/Issued 1244 PM MST Thu Nov 26 2026/ 

Meteorological Overview:

Strengthening zonal flow aloft and a tightening surface pressure 
gradient are already driving gusty winds along the Rocky Mountain 
Front this morning as a fast-moving shortwave and Pacific moisture
push into the Northern Rockies. Mountain wave activity will help 
spread strong winds onto the adjacent plains later today, with gusts
exceeding 70 mph along the immediate eastern slopes before a secondary
mountain wave redevelops near the Rocky Mountain Front this evening
and gradually weakens toward Friday morning. Farther east, most plains
locations remain breezy to gusty below warning thresholds, while Judith
Basin County holds onto a more persistent pressure gradient and mountain
wave risk from this afternoon into early Friday afternoon. Even after
High Wind Warnings expire across the Rocky Mountain Front and Hi-Line
Friday morning, deeper daytime mixing Friday afternoon will keep winds
brisk across the plains before tapering off around sunset. 

Pacific moisture accompanying today's wave will bring precipitation
to the Continental Divide from this afternoon into early Friday 
morning, mainly along the northern Rocky Mountain Front. Precipitation
starts as a rain-snow mix before transitioning to snow, with 2 to 4
inches expected over Marias Pass and 6 to 10 inches on the higher peaks.
Lower elevations may briefly see a mix with limited impacts, and strong
downsloping will create a sharp cutoff in moisture south and east of
Marias Pass. 

Attention then turns to an upper-level shortwave diving southeastward
out of British Columbia late Friday into Saturday, inducing a surface
low south of the Montana border that tracks due east from Idaho into
Wyoming. As zonal flow develops aloft and a tighter thermal gradient
sets up on the northern side of the low, low- to mid- level shear aligns
straight east-to-west, creating potential for stationary, training
snow bands and localized frontogenesis across southwest Montana. 
Snow levels start around 5,000 to 6,000 feet Friday afternoon 
before dropping to valley floors by Saturday morning, though 
precipitation tapers off quickly by mid-morning. Where heavier 
bands organize, dynamic cooling will help temperatures fall faster
and support heavy snowfall rates at times, even at lower 
elevations. Once the system exits and colder air rushes in 
Saturday morning, rapidly dropping temperatures will quickly 
freeze lingering wet snow and slush on roadways. 

Ridging builds east across the region on Sunday before weakening as
zonal flow and Pacific moisture return. Early Sunday stays dry, 
leading into an unsettled start to next week with near- average 
temperatures and mainly light precipitation favored near the 
Continental Divide. 

Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

High Wind Warnings remain on track through Friday morning along 
the Rocky Mountain Front and adjacent plains, and through early 
Friday afternoon for Judith Basin County. While Cascade County was
evaluated for potential expansion, morning soundings show 30 to 
40 kt flow around 700mb separated from the surface by low-level 
inversions, and the strongest pressure gradient this afternoon 
does not align well with stronger winds aloft near sunset. As a 
result, Cascade County remains out of the warning for now, though 
trends and observations will continue to be monitored. Similarly, 
despite models hinting at near-criteria gusts via efficient 
daytime mixing Friday afternoon after warnings expire, confidence 
is too low to extend headlines at this time. 

A Winter Weather Advisory is in effect for the East Glacier and 
Marias Pass area through early Friday morning, with high 
confidence in impacts remaining confined near the pass and higher 
terrain due to the sharp precipitation cutoff to the south and 
east. 

For the Friday night into Saturday morning system across 
southwest Montana, Winter Weather Advisories have been issued to 
cover the combination of impactful pass snowfall, heavy snow at 
times, and rapidly falling temperatures. While overall snowfall 
totals are expected to remain below Winter Storm Warning criteria,
European EFI values exceeding 0.8 for QPF and snowfall highlight 
the upper- end potential if frontogenesis and east-to-west 
training bands lock in over a particular corridor. Where those 
bands organize, dynamic cooling and higher snowfall rates will 
drive rapid transitions to wet valley snow, followed by a quick 
freeze-up Saturday morning as temperatures drop sharply behind the
departing low.
